545b27fd785d6a72: LILLE, Sept 21 — A group of masked robbers broke into the French home of a family and, during an overnight ordeal, forced them to transfer €40,000 (RM183,000) in cryptocurrency, a local prosecutor said Sunday.

The family – a couple and their two children, aged 8 and 12 – had to be treated by paramedics for shock after the robbers left their home in Vendin le Vieil, a village on the outskirts of the northern city of Lens.
Police were hunting the gang of four criminals who carried out the robbery, prosecutor Etienne Thieffry said.
The father in the family worked in the technology sector, the prosecutor said.

France has in the past couple of years experienced a wave of robberies targeting owners of cryptocurrency, which is stored digitally and whose ownership and transfer is difficult or impossible to trace.
In the first six months of this year, 77 such crimes were recorded, a significant jump on the same period last year.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez in June vowed to boost security for people working in the crypto sector. — AFP
66c845a775ebcbe0: SINGAPORE, Sept 21 — A 90‑year‑old Singapore man has failed in his bid to obtain spousal maintenance from his 89‑year‑old ex‑wife, after the Family Justice Courts found that both parties were already adequately provided for following the division of their matrimonial assets.

In a judgment published on Sept 16, the court noted that the former couple — married for more than 64 years — will each walk away with significant sums from their matrimonial pool, largely derived from their S$5.8 million (RM18.5 million) home. The wife will receive about S$3.5 million, while the husband will obtain S$2.4 million.

Justice Dedar Singh Gill said the husband’s share of more than S$2 million was “more than sufficient to meet the needs of a 90‑year‑old retiree for the remainder of his life”, adding that both parties have no earning capacity and rely solely on pensions or payouts.

The court found that the wife had contributed the greater share to the marriage, both financially and through caregiving. She financed their homes, paid household bills, covered property taxes up to 2024, and supported the family on her pension after retiring in 1992 — giving her husband half of her monthly payout.

She also produced detailed evidence of her role as the primary caregiver, managing the household, supervising domestic workers, and overseeing the children’s schooling and activities. The husband, the judge noted, offered only general assertions of involvement without specifics.
The court ultimately assessed indirect contributions at 70:30 in her favour, leading to an overall division ratio of 60:40.

The man had sought maintenance as an incapacitated former husband, citing medical issues, minimal income, and the financial burden of living alone in the matrimonial home. He also asked for a lump sum amounting to 5–10 per cent of his share of the assets if maintenance was denied.
Justice Gill rejected both requests, ruling that ordering maintenance from an elderly retiree living on a pension would not be “just or necessary”.
The judge ordered that property tax for 2025 and 2026 be borne equally, noting that while the husband should not shoulder the entire bill, his argument for the wife to pay it fully was untenable.
The couple must sell their home on the open market within six months, with joint conduct of the sale. Each party will bear their own legal costs.
bb05cf9f31245690: SEPTEMBER 21 — As a schoolboy, there was one shirt I desperately wanted to wear.
It was not particularly fashionable. In fact, it was simply a blue school uniform shirt.

But in my secondary school, that blue shirt belonged to the librarians. They stood out from the rest of us, and to me they represented something rather special. I hoped that one day I would be chosen to wear it too.
I never was. At the time, it felt like a small disappointment. Looking back now, however, I realise that not wearing the blue shirt mattered very little.
The librarians I admired all those years ago gave me something far more enduring than a different coloured uniform: They quietly taught me to keep looking.
Even as a young student, I was happiest whenever I found myself surrounded by books. Storybooks, science fiction, comics, travel writing, history and geography all competed for my attention.

Among my favourite places was the reference section, especially the Encyclopaedia Britannica. I could spend hours reading its entries, not because I was searching for a particular answer, but because one topic would naturally lead me to another. Curiosity seemed to have a way of choosing its own direction.
There was no internet then. There were simply books, curiosity and time.
When I entered Universiti Malaya, that habit continued almost without my noticing. The Main Library felt enormous, with its shelves stretching across three floors.
I often arrived looking for a particular book or journal, only to leave having discovered several others I had not intended to read.
Looking back, I realise the library was quietly teaching me that learning rarely follows a straight line. Sometimes the most valuable discoveries begin with a question we never intended to ask.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The librarians I admired all those years ago gave me something far more enduring than a different coloured uniform: They quietly taught me to keep looking. — Unsplash pic
Years later, as a lecturer and researcher, the medical library became almost a second workplace. Research was very different in those days.
We searched card catalogues, walked patiently through rows of bound journals and photocopied the articles we needed.
When a journal was unavailable locally, we submitted requests through the inter-library network and waited, sometimes for weeks, hoping the paper would eventually arrive.
By today’s standards, the process seems slow. Yet I do not remember it as frustrating. I remember it as purposeful.
The librarians were always there to help us navigate the ever-growing world of knowledge.
They knew where information might be found, but more importantly, they encouraged us not to stop searching simply because an answer was not immediately available.

Over the years, the library itself continued to evolve. Book talks brought authors into conversation with readers. Exhibitions celebrated not only academic achievements but also photography, art and creative work across the university community.
One programme that particularly stayed with me was the Human Library, where instead of borrowing a book, we listened to someone share the story of their own life.
I remember listening to Sister Mathina Bee Gulam, a retired nurse who had served in humanitarian missions and refugee settings.
Her experiences could certainly have been written down, but hearing them directly from the person who had lived them was something altogether different.
That afternoon reminded me that learning does not exist only between the covers of a book. Sometimes it is found in another person’s experiences, generously shared.
Looking back, I realise these programmes were never simply about expanding library services.
They reflected a much deeper understanding of what a library is meant to do. A library is not merely a place where knowledge is stored. It is a place where curiosity continues to grow.

Today, almost every journal article, textbook and scientific paper can be reached within seconds. Information has become astonishingly accessible, and researchers like myself have benefited enormously from these advances.
Yet easy access to information does not automatically make us lifelong learners. Information answers the questions we already know to ask. Curiosity encourages us to ask the next question.
That is the quiet lesson libraries have been teaching all along.
As technology changes, libraries will undoubtedly continue to change with it. Shelves may become smaller, digital collections will continue to expand, and new ways of sharing knowledge will emerge.

None of these developments concern me particularly. The true measure of a library has never been the number of books it holds, but whether it continues to nurture minds that remain open, inquisitive and eager to learn.
Sometimes I think back to that blue shirt I so badly wanted to wear as a schoolboy. I never became one of the librarians who wore it.
Yet, over the course of a lifetime, I have come to appreciate what they quietly represented.

They were not simply looking after books. They were looking after something much more precious: a place where generations of students, researchers and readers could continue asking questions long after their formal education had ended.

Perhaps that is why libraries continue to matter so deeply, regardless of how much technology changes. They remind us that learning is never really about reaching the final answer. It is about preserving the desire to keep looking.

* Ng Kwan Hoong is an Emeritus Professor of Biomedical Imaging at the Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Malaya. A 2020 Merdeka Award recipient, he is a medical physicist by training but also enjoys writing, drawing, listening to classical music, and bridging the gap between older and younger generations. He may be reached at ngkh@ummc.edu.my

fd3ed8256d970a21: TORONTO, Sept 21 — Spain’s The Black Ball, a gay rights drama set during the country’s civil war, won top prize Sunday at the Toronto International Film Festival.
The ambitious epic, known as La Bola Negra in Spanish, stars Miguel Bernardeau, along with Penelope Cruz and Glenn Close, weaving the stories of three gay men across different eras in Spain.

The Toronto win gives the film, directed by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, a creative duo affectionately known as “Los Javis,” an early boost in the race for recognition at the Oscars, where the festival’s People’s Choice Award has proved a useful bellwether.

Speaking to reporters earlier this month, Ambrossi, who used to be in a relationship with Calvo, called The Black Ball “a tribute to the LGBTQ+ community” of the past that fought for human rights and an “epic gay drama for everyone.”
Unlike festival prizes bestowed by Cannes and Venice, the Toronto People’s Choice Award is selected by public audiences.
Any movie in the festival’s official lineup is eligible, unlike the curated “in competition” shortlists used elsewhere.

Ambrossi and Calvo are famous in Spain particularly for their television work, but their star has been rising globally after a smash debut of the film at Cannes, where it shared the best director award with Pawel Pawlikowski (Fatherland).
Early inspiration for the movie came from the unpublished play written by Federico Garcia Lorca, a poet who was executed by fascist forces at the beginning of the Spanish Civil War in 1936.
The directors said the four pages of unfinished writing sparked their curiosity and drew them in.
“We got obsessed with his work,” Calvo told journalists, adding he and Ambrossi immersed themselves in Lorca’s writings, correspondence and biographies.
The filmmakers said that many countries still have anti-LGBTQ laws and people within the community can be persecuted or even killed for their sexuality.
Calvo emphasized that the film is “about empathy and humanity and seeing the other as a person.” — AFP
c8a4d022cfc05e2c: SINGAPORE, Sept 21 — Singapore police are warning the public about a re-emerging phishing scam that uses the Singapore Police Force (SPF) logo to frighten victims into handing over their bank details.

According to a police statement issued on September 20, scammers have been circulating pop-up alerts that mimic official SPF branding. These alerts falsely claim that a victim’s computer or mobile device has been locked due to repeated access of websites containing illegal content. Victims are then told they must pay “outstanding fines” within hours to unlock their devices.
A countdown timer to heighten panic
A payment form requesting bank card details
Victims typically discover they have been scammed only after unauthorised foreign currency charges appear on their bank accounts — often exceeding the supposed fines.

Authorities stressed that the SPF does not remotely lock personal devices and does not issue fines through pop-up messages. They urged the public to remain vigilant and verify suspicious alerts by calling the ScamShield Helpline at 1799.

The warning comes amid a broader rise in impersonation scams, where criminals use official logos, government branding, or spoofed websites to deceive victims. Police continue to advise the public to avoid clicking on unexpected pop-ups, refrain from entering banking details on unfamiliar sites, and report suspicious activity promptly.
2ecdbb0926113ba3: LOS ANGELES, Sept 21— Resident Evil, a horror movie based on a video game franchise, swept the North American box office with (US$60 million; RM245.1 million) opening weekend, industry estimates showed Sunday.
The Sony-distributed movie is directed by Zach Cregger and stars Austin Abrams, who plays a medical courier battling mutant creatures to deliver a package to a remote hospital.
Resident Evil displaced last week’s top performer, Warner Bros’ Practical Magic 2, a long-awaited sequel starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, into a distant second place.

bb539c9b4ab678d2: ASIA IN BRIEF Chinese memory-maker CXMT, whose products Apple has reportedly evaluated to use in the iPhone, claims to have made a miniaturization breakthrough. The company on Sunday posted news that it has started mass production of chips made with a fifth-generation process that essentially doubles memory density, meaning it can cut twice the number of dies for memory chips from a single wafer. CXMT says its key breakthrough is a high-k dielectric metal gate process – a way of insulating silicon to improve efficiency – adapted to baking DRAM. The company claims its new process puts it on par with rival memory-makers. The proof of the pudding is apparently a pair of LPDDR5X memory modules for smartphones or other high-end consumer electronics. Both products boast 24GB of memory. If CXMT’s claims of improved density and mass production are correct – and the new products aren’t too pricey – it’s good news for Chinese electronics manufacturers who, like their global peers, are struggling to source affordable memory thanks to supply chain crunches caused by demand for AI-related products. That shortage recently saw Apple hike iPhone prices by $100 and led the GSM Association to warn that rising smartphone prices threaten to slow digital inclusion. Democratic governments, however, are mostly uncomfortable with allowing their smartphone manufacturers to use Chinese components. India starts charging fees for instant payments India’s National Payments Corporation (NCP) last week introduced fees to use its Unified Payments Interface (UPI) for the first time. UPI is an instant payment scheme provided by India’s government. It allows transfer of funds between participants, which include over 700 local banks and many e-wallet providers. It also allows person-to-person payments. The scheme is a ubiquitous option even at small retailers across India, and one of the world’s busiest payment schemes with over 24 billion monthly transactions. The scheme is so popular that other payment providers outside India have adopted it so that Indian tourists can use it abroad. UPI launched in 2016 and has until now been free for shoppers and merchants alike. The NCP last week announced it will soon require merchants to pay 0.4 percent fee for when taking payments above 2,000 rupees (£15; $21). India’s government said the charge is needed to fund the operation of the scheme, the cost of which is currently borne by the nation’s government and participating financial institutions. The government ordered merchants not to pass on the fee. China’s online reach is surprisingly short, researcher finds China’s share of content distribution networks is small, leaving Asian nations largely dependent on US companies. That’s the key finding of research by Jason Hung, a quantitative sociologist and research fellow at the Internet Society’s Pulse program. Hung looked up the top 1,000 most popular websites in ten southeast Asian countries (Cambodia, China, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Viet Nam) using Google’s Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX), then used three different CDN and IP infrastructure lookup approaches to identify the company and jurisdiction serving the content. “I then used the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) to quantify the severity of market concentration (by service provider and by jurisdiction), where a score above 2,500 is considered highly concentrated, and a maximum score (10,000) means a single actor serves an entire market.” That approach led to the finding that “content delivery in SEA is highly concentrated, with HHI scores ranging from 8,950 to 10,000 across all ten countries.” The researcher found that China-registered companies held no more than 3.9 percent of the CDN market between 2024 and 2026, and that US-registered companies dominated, ranging from 95.9 percent to 99.6 percent. “These findings go beyond what I expected based on my understanding of China’s control over the Global South, especially in Southeast Asia,” he wrote, and leave organizations across the region highly dependent on US tech companies to expose their content to the wider internet. Toyota to hire 400,000 robots Japanese auto-maker Toyota last week told investors it plans to hire 400,000 robots that have two-fingered “hands.” The Embodied Learning robot for Enhanced Yield, aka “ELEY,” is capable of folding a t-shirt and learning how to perform tasks that require considerable manual dexterity. Apparently, the bots needed two weeks to learn how to fold a tee. Readers who are parents of teenaged children might find that speed interesting. Toyota plans to deploy the bots alongside human workers in its own factories, where they will be free to move about using either a battery or an extension cord as an energy source. The company hopes its partners will also employ ELEY. India has five functional fabs The government of India last week announced that the nation is now home to five functioning semiconductor fabrication plants and said its latest industry promotion scheme has drawn $12 billion of investment. Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw said India hopes to create “a complete semiconductor ecosystem” but offered no information about the nation’s attempts to create indigenous processors for local use. Vaishnaw last year said work is under way to produce a 7nm processor as part of India’s Shakti project, which aims to enable the country to produce its own servers and even supercomputers. Status updates on that effort are few and far between, and the project is yet to produce a modern microprocessor suitable for use in a personal device or server. ®
2a36ec411fafb778: Malaysia Day celebrations every September carry a distinct resonance in Sabah and Sarawak. In these two states, unity is not merely a political slogan, but a lived reality. Inter-ethnic and inter-religious frictions are remarkably rare; instead, Bumiputera and non-Bumiputera communities coexist seamlessly as a cohesive people.
While various historical and cultural factors contribute to this social harmony, the most powerful catalyst hiding in plain sight is a linguistic one: the Malay language.
In West Malaysia, linguistic and social circles can remain highly segregated among people, but East Malaysia’s unique demographic tapestry demands a universal bridge.

Sabah and Sarawak are home to dozens of indigenous ethnic groups, including the Kadazan-Dusun, Murut, Iban, and Bidayuh. No single indigenous language dominates the landscape. Malay naturally evolved into the ultimate daily lingua franca, spoken by all and sundry, transcending ethnic divides.

This linguistic embrace is particularly evident among East Malaysia's non-Bumiputera communities, primarily the Chinese. While their counterparts in Peninsular Malaysia often rely on Mandarin, Cantonese, or Hokkien for intra-ethnic communication and may hesitate when speaking the national language, non-Bumiputera in East Malaysia demonstrate remarkable fluency and spontaneity in Malay.

This regional divergence is deeply rooted in the phonetic accessibility of East Malaysian Malay. Structurally, the variants spoken in the East are closer to standard written Malay, making them significantly more intuitive for non-native speakers to master.

For instance, while the standard Peninsular dialect modifies the final "a" into a schwa sound (turning saya into say-uh), Sabahan and Sarawakian Malay preserve the clean, phonetic "a" sound (say-ah). By largely speaking the language exactly as it is written, East Malaysians bypass the pressure of navigating complex vowel shifts or exclusionary slang rules.
Furthermore, the language in East Malaysia has evolved organically into a living, breathing community identity rather than a rigid, institutional subject.

Rather than sticking strictly to textbook constraints, communities speak distinct regional dialects heavily infused with localised slang, indigenous loanwords, and Chinese particle markers. Whether it is the ubiquitous Sabahan "bah" or the distinct Sarawakian pronouns "kamek" and "kitak," this blending strips away structural formality and fosters an authentic, shared ownership of the language.

This linguistic integration is further cemented by the high rates of intermarriage that define East Malaysian society. With far more interracial families than the Peninsula, it is incredibly common for Chinese-Bumiputera households to speak Malay natively at home. This blending effectively blurs the strict cultural and linguistic boundaries seen elsewhere in the country.

Ultimately, the Malay language in Sabah and Sarawak does not just connect different communities; it unites them. By transforming the national language into an accessible, organic, and inclusive medium, East Malaysians offer a profound blueprint for what true national unity can look like.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

75c6b50e993ab161: Pasti bukan mudah buat PMX terima peletakan jawatan Lok Siew Fook.
Jika saya perdana menteri (sekadar perasan dan berangan) saya juga tidak mahu melepaskannya.

Ini kerana Loke is a good and hard working minister. Dan bijak. Peletakan jawatannya sebagai menteri pengangkutan is a loss to the government and by extension to the country. Suka Loke atau tidak, sayang DAP partinya atau benci DAP, begitulah realiti.
Namun letak jawatan hasrat Loke and endorsed by the DAP Central Executive Committee. Lantas mesti dihormati.

“Kami sedar ada parti parti di luar sana menunggu DAP keluar kerajaan supaya mereka boleh cetus ketidakstabilan politik dan menyebabkan Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim hilang sokongan majoriti kemudian bubar Parlimen.
"Ini yang diingini pihak lawan. (Jadi kami) tak mahu beri peluru kepada mereka”, kata Loke pada sidang media selepas mesyuarat Jawatankuasa Tertinggi Pusat (CEC) DAP pada Sabtu.
Ertinya, menurut Loke, partinya tidak mahu 'layan provokasi' pihak lawan.
Provokasi pernah juga dibuat berikutan persembahan hambar DAP pada PRN Sabah, Johor dan Negeri Sembilan lalu yang 'memaksa' parti pimpinan Loke mengadakan sidang khas 16 Ogos lalu.

Loke selaku setiausaha agung DAP duduk dalam Majlis Presiden Pakatan Harapan yang berpegang kepada pendirian bahawa tiada siapa yang mengatasi undang undang dan sesiapa sahaja yang disabitkan kesalahan perlu menjalani hukuman mengikut lunas undang undang seperti mana yang termaktub dalam Perlembagaan Persekutuan.

Ertinya, DAP berpendirian sama dengan Majlis Presiden PH. This is obviously stating the obvious. Dan dalam tidak mahu layan provokasi pesaing-pesaing politiknya menurut Loke, 'pada masa sama kami ada pendirian tersendiri (berhubung pengampunan bersyarat Najib) yang dizahirkan menerusi tawaran saya untuk letak jawatan'.
DAP bagaimanapun menurut Loke menghormati keputusan Yang di-Pertuan Agong. Bagi saya, ini boleh dieksploitasi parti lawan.
Loke menyifatkan langkah partinya sesuatu yang 'bertanggungjawab'. Hanya beliau seorang letak jawatan, kata Loke, bagi memastikan kerajaan kekal stabil.
Tetapi jika semua anggota Jemaah Menteri dari DAP letak jawatan, ini boleh membawa risiko atau ruang kerajaan tumbang seperti yang diharapkan pihak lawan.
Oleh itu, kata Loke, CEC buat keputusan mereka kekal dalam Jemaah Menteri, 'walaupun mereka juga sedia pada mana mana waktu, apa apa ketika (untuk melepaskan jawatan)'.
Sudah tentu golongan yang bukan peminat besar DAP tidak puas hati dengan penjelasan Loke.
Antaranya, Ketua Pemuda Umno Akmal Saleh yang menyifatkan perkembangan membabitkan DAP ibarat 'order lain, yang sampai lain', merujuk isu Timbalan Pengerusi Kebangsaan Ng Kor Ming.

Kawan baiknya masa kini, Pengarah Pilihan Raya PAS Sanusi Nor memperlekehkan langkah DAP, dengan berkata: "Dulu Nga kata macam tu juga, tak letak (jawatan) pun. Acah-acah tarik tali. Politik mercun papan. Pong pang ping pang lepas itu senyap."
Menurut saya, kata-kata itu cuma preemptive move – untuk memastikan Loke letak jawatan.
Bekas Ahli Parlimen Subang daripada PKR Wong Chen mempersoalkan mengapa Loke ambil tanggungjawab dan mahu letak jawatan, bukan Hannah Yeoh dan Nga.

Yeoh ialah anggota Lembaga Pengampunan Wilayah Persekutuan selaku menteri Wilayah Persekutuan manakala Nga pernah menyatakan akan letak jawatan menteri perumahan dan kerajaan tempatan jika Najib dibebaskan.
Untuk berlaku adil, perlu ditegaskan sekali lagi bahawa Najib diberi pengampunan bersyarat dan dizin ditahan di rumah. Ertinya, beliau 'tidak dibebaskan'.

Manakala Yeoh menegaskan beliau telah menyatakan kepada lembaga pengampunan pandangannya 'secara jujur, berterus-terang dan berlandaskan hati nurani demi kepentingan negara', serta berdasarkan pendapat undang undang 'setelah meneliti pendapat bertulis peguam negara'.
Apa pun kritikan, serangan dan provokasi pesaing serta pembenci DAP tercetus pantas. Lihat sahaja komen di media sosial dan ruang komen pembaca portal berita. Banyak juga berbaur perkauman.

Sebagai parti politik, tidak boleh dinafikan apa yang dilakukan DAP dan Loke mempunyai elemen kepentingan parti dan kelangsungan politik. Ada penganalis dipetik FMT berpendapat keputusan Loke mungkin tidak dapat reda kemarahan akar umbi DAP terhadap pengampunan bersyarat Najib.

Lau Zhe Wei dari Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia dipetik berkata, peletakan jawatan beramai-ramai (yakni semua anggota Jemaah Menteri daripada DAP) ialah langkah wajar meskipun DAP tidak bertanggungjawab terhadap pengampunan bersyarat Najib.

Bagi saya, DAP telah menyatakan pendiriannya loud and clear. Ada pemerhati politik beritahu saya, "That’s a strategic withdrawal tactic from Loke and DAP to move forward and to placate the Chinese anger."

Saya setuju ia bertujuan menenangkan hati masyarakat Cina yang rata-rata yakin Najib sudah diberi pengadilan secukupnya lalu mesti pay for his crime. Berdasarkan keputusan mahkamah. Majoriti rakyat Malaysia sependapat.

Bak kata Dr Mahathir Mohamad, Najib sudah diadili oleh Mahkamah Tinggi, Mahkamah Rayuan dan Mahkamah Persekutuan, membabitkan sembilan hakim yang mendapati beliau bersalah (dalam kes SRC International).
Seorang lagi pemerhati politik berkata, keputusan Loke 'is a good move. At least good for DAP supporters'. Maksudnya, penyokong yang bukan ahli parti. Rakyat biasa yang sokong DAP.
Yang jelas, Loke memikul tanggungjawab selaku ketua DAP.

Untuk menutup penulisan kali ini, saya petik catatan Facebook kawan lama Kassim Muhamad, seorang aktivis seni: "Lain padang lain belalang, lain pemimpin politik lain cara melihat tanggungjawab dan pertanggungjawaban. Pengundi bolehlah menilai bagaimana dan kenapa pemimpin politik kekadang tidak sama cara dan tindakannya bila berdepan dengan isu tanggungjawab."
Memang betul, saudara.

d7acaafcd717f3c8: I've spent years building robots that replaced human workers, so I'm no stranger to technological fear, but even I did a double take last week.

On Sept 9, Jacob Coxon, who spent the past three years at OpenAI and then Anthropic, quit with a post on X that has since been viewed more than 100 million times: "Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

And lest you think this was just one disgruntled ex-employee, Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment science team, agreed that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans", putting the odds at more than 10% within the next decade.
But others working in the AI arena see this as fear mongering and a possible sales pitch.
Let me lay out, as fairly as I can, what each camp believes.

Start with the worried camp, who call themselves safety researchers and get called doomers, whose case rests on three planks. The first is that AI capability is climbing faster than our ability to contain it, which is why Coxon warns of "superhuman systems that can hack anything" that will "acquire real power and resources".

The second plank is that the machines are already gaming us. In July, OpenAI ran an internal model through hacking exercises in which, investigators estimate, 30% to 40% of the tasks were impossible. Rather than fail, roughly 1,200 AI agents turned a shared file store into a secret message board, exchanged more than 70,000 messages, faked answers and researched how to tamper with their own transcripts.

About 700 of them then broke into Hugging Face, an external AI hosting company. Investigators at Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) and Redwood Research found that the agents had "realised this activity was out of scope and unethical" but joined anyway.

The podcaster Dwarkesh Patel, whose essay on the affair went viral, argued in a reply to a critic who said this hacking was "small potatoes" that within years we'll have "hundreds of millions of much smarter AIs". He added that if those AIs were as willing to coordinate in secret to fool us, humanity would be in the position of the Mughals once the East India Company got a foothold in India.

The third plank is the warning and request for guardrails by AI industry leaders. In May 2023, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis signed a statement ranking AI extinction risk alongside "pandemics and nuclear war"; that same month Altman urged the United States Senate to consider "licensing and testing requirements" for models "above a threshold of capabilities".
Now the rebuttal of the other camp, which runs from Silicon Valley's accelerationists to sceptics like Gary Marcus, comes in three parts too. The first is that the fear mongering is a business model.

David Sacks, then the White House AI czar, said last October that "Anthropic is running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering", and Stanford's Andrew Ng wrote that proprietary providers "would hate to have to compete with free, opensource software, and have lobbied intensely for regulations to kneecap it".
Amodei calls such claims "inaccurate" and says his proposals would spare smaller labs.

The second part is to read the July incident again, minus the dramatic language. Marcus points out that the agents got into Hugging Face through API keys left in public code repositories, and that OpenAI had given thousands of agents write access to a shared directory. He concluded that "the scandal is the inept in-house security at OpenAI".

In this telling, a badly designed exam with unlocked doors produced cheating, not Skynet. In case you missed the Terminator movies, Skynet is the fictional AI system that triggers a global nuclear war.

The third part is what caution costs. A licence written in Washington binds only American companies, as June showed: the US Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to cut off foreign nationals from Claude Fable 5, and the model went dark worldwide for nearly three weeks while every rival, OpenAI included, carried on.

Stanford's 2026 AI Index puts the best Chinese model a mere 2.7% behind America's best, and DeepSeek's top model charges RM16 per million output tokens to Anthropic's whopping RM204, so a pause, this camp says, is a gift to China.

There's also what a pause would leave undiscovered, because AI is already saving lives, not merely promising to, they argue. Google DeepMind's AlphaFold, an AI that works out the three-dimensional shape of proteins, the starting point for new drugs, mapped 200 million of them and won its creators a Nobel Prize.

Then there's personalised cancer care. Moderna and Merck's melanoma vaccine is built for each patient, whose tumour is sequenced so an algorithm can pick up to 34 of its mutations to target. Those who received it alongside immunotherapy had a 49% lower risk of recurrence or death after five years in an early trial, a finding a 1,137-patient Phase 3 trial backed last month.

On the ward, a University of California San Diego AI that watches vital signs and lab results for the first stirrings of sepsis cut deaths from it by 17%, and AI-assisted screening of more than 100,000 Swedish women caught 29% more breast cancers with 44% less radiologist work.
The sceptics ask: What if pausing or slowing down AI progress delays the development of such essential life-saving technologies?

Both camps agree this is the most powerful technology of our lifetimes, and both read the same 70,000 messages those OpenAI agents exchanged in July. One saw a machine learning to conspire; the other saw a lab that forgot to lock its doors.

Whether AI is a tool to be governed or an agent to be feared, and whether the people asking for the brakes should be the ones holding them, is the question that decides everything else, and it deserves a column of its own. Stay tuned.

653144da3f9afc34: From Terence Netto
Hassan Karim's opinion that the conditional pardon for Najib Razak is a “golden opportunity” for Pakatan Harapan, deserves attention – and, more pointedly, exploitation.

Since last November, PH and its component parties have been reeling from electoral setbacks in Sabah, Johor and Negeri Sembilan. Rubbing salt into the wound was the glee displayed by its erstwhile partner Umno over the PH defeats.

It was particularly galling in Negeri Sembilan, where the PKR-led state government was toppled and DAP’s Loke Siew Fook defeated at the hands of an MCA opponent who was cheered on by none other than Umno chief Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
The fact that Zahid sits next to Loke in the Cabinet did not give the Umno president pause in his quest of electoral spoils. Apparently, all is fair and foul in Cabinet and on the hustings.
If Zahid lacks esprit de corps, PH need not bother about decorum in seeking to exploit Najib’s conditional pardon for electoral advantage.
Equality under the law

However one looks at the pardon and the house arrest arrangement for Najib, it sits ill with ordinary people, who are apt to think that there is one rule for the super-elite and another for the hoi polloi.
This is despite the fact that many people think Najib was a good prime minister, especially during the first 18 months after he took over from Abdullah Ahmad Badawi in 2009.
Nothing grates more on ordinary people’s sense of being underprivileged than seeing the guarantee of equal treatment before the law honoured more in the breach than in the observance.
Also, Umno’s decision to organise a fundraiser for Najib to pay his RM50 million fine in order to fulfil a condition of his house arrest must rank as a faux pas of disastrous proportions.
It is like asking victims to help pay the fine imposed on a felon caught with his hands in the public till.
Public morality

Because the issue of Najib Razak and his responsibility for the financial scandals arising from the 1MDB imbroglio involves questions of public morality and accountability, it is heartening to hear what Amanah deputy president Mujahid Yusof Rawa has said.
Amanah has not particularly distinguished itself in handling these issues because of the space it has conceded to PAS and its president, Abdul Hadi Awang, who have ruled the rhetorical roost.

At any one time, it is difficult to sort out what the PAS supremo is actually saying because his writings and speeches are clouded in jargon. Listeners give up, if for no other reason than that the subject matter has to do with Islam, a subject about which a non-Muslim, especially, must tread with caution.

So, when Mujahid, in criticising Umno and PAS for celebrating the grant of a conditional pardon to Najib, spoke of the tawdriness of the moral compass of both parties, he employed a clarity that was the reverse of Hadi’s opacity.
“What has happened to the moral compass of our Malay people?” Mujahid said.

“It’s time the Malays made an important decision for the sake of their dignity. Don’t allow Malay dignity to be represented by those who normalise crime, otherwise our future generations will consider corruption as heroics for the Malay people,” the Amanah leader said plaintively.
PH has been on the back foot for some years now, a consequence of Anwar Ibrahim’s strange loss of effectiveness and clarity of vision.
The “golden opportunity” presented by Najib’s conditional pardon and Umno’s fundraising are a shot in the foot by Umno and PAS that PH must exploit to the hilt.
A gift horse is not to be looked at in the mouth.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

6563681e21fb3442: In January, US president Donald Trump suggested that his newly created Board of Peace might eventually replace the United Nations. It’s easy to dismiss this as Trump’s typical bluster, but it also underscores the UN’s loss of credibility.
The problem is that the world still desperately needs an institution capable of bringing countries together to tackle global challenges like climate change.

Amid escalating geopolitical rivalries, Security Council paralysis, funding cuts, and the growing willingness of countries like the US to disengage from multilateral institutions, almost every UN mandate is under strain.
Whoever succeeds António Guterres as secretary-general in January will need to work with member states to restore confidence in the UN’s ability to act and show that multilateralism can still work.
The UN remains the closest thing the world has to a universal forum. Its legitimacy rests on the scope of its membership. But legitimacy does not guarantee credibility.

To prove itself worthy of the role the world needs it to play, the UN must demonstrate that multilateral processes can be transparent, that commitments can be enforced, and that those who make the rules can be held accountable.

This credibility test begins with the process for choosing the next secretary-general. While candidates vying to replace Guterres have published detailed vision statements and faced questions from civil-society groups, the decision remains largely opaque, with the Security Council’s five permanent members wielding outsize influence.

The irony is striking: the UN is asking the world to trust multilateral institutions, yet its most important appointment is decided behind closed doors. How leaders are chosen affects their credibility once in office, making it essential that the process itself be free of conflicts of interest.

The same applies to collective negotiations. While the 2015 Paris climate agreement remains the broadest pact the UN has ever brokered, its largely non-binding structure has left implementation dependent on governments’ willingness to follow through on their pledges.

A decade later, that willingness has been no match for the industries working to impede climate action. The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) still lacks clear, system-wide rules for identifying and managing conflicts of interest, and fossil-fuel interests continue to influence climate negotiations with little scrutiny.

Research by Transparency International found that more than half of the participants at last year’s UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Belém did not fully disclose their institutional affiliations.

Guterres has used his tenure to push for climate action, criticising the fossil-fuel industry for expanding production despite knowing that its business model was incompatible with human survival, and has called for a windfall tax on oil and gas profits. But even that is not enough.

With the UN Environment Programme warning that, at the current rate, the global-warming threshold of 1.5° Celsius will be breached within three years, the stakes are too high not to know who shapes the world’s response—and to what end.

The next secretary-general won’t have the authority to set conflict-of-interest rules for the UNFCCC process; such rules are for governments to negotiate and adopt. But that does not mean the secretary-general is powerless.

The position’s public platform and influence across the UN system could be used to press governments and COP presidencies for tougher integrity standards, thereby making it clear that the credibility of the UN’s climate efforts depends on the credibility of those given a seat at the negotiating table.

Collective action is also needed to tackle high-level corruption, state capture, and the global networks that conceal illicit wealth. International rules are only as effective as the governments willing to implement them and the institutions enforcing them. Both sets of actors can be compromised by the very interests they’re supposed to regulate.
The UN Convention against Corruption remains one of the most important global frameworks for setting common standards and holding governments to them.

The next phase of its review in Vienna, which will focus on criminalisation and enforcement, offers a unique opportunity to bolster its accountability mechanisms. But for it to succeed, governments must allow their own records to be scrutinised.

These are not separate problems. Whether it is fossil-fuel interests compromising the COP process, the UN’s corruption framework going unenforced, or the Security Council being paralysed by great-power interests, the question is the same: Does multilateralism still have teeth, or can governments ignore its rules without consequence?

The next secretary-general cannot answer that question alone. But they can decide to spend their political capital on making transparency a top priority, pushing conflicts of interest into the open before they become scandals, and pressuring governments to keep their promises.

History offers plenty of precedents. From Dag Hammarskjöld to Kofi A Annan, secretaries-general have repeatedly exercised influence well beyond their formal mandates by building political credibility and personal authority.

While candidates in this round have spoken about efficiency, preventive diplomacy, and restoring confidence in the UN, they have said far less about how they would ensure transparency and hold member states to account.

To rebuild credibility, the UN must start from within. That means greater openness about how decisions are made, how resources are used, and how commitments are implemented. With trust in multilateralism already in decline, the UN must hold itself to the same standards it expects of others.
Maíra Martini is CEO of Transparency International.

Ferrari followed with its first true four-seater, the all-wheel drive FF, which adopted "Breadvan" styling. Its first hatchback was still a three-door, though, and slightly more practical for carrying cargo rather than humans in the rear. That was true for the GTC4 that followed, too. But with the Purosangue, the rear passengers have been given something of an upgrade.

c76e20d9149fa760: For most of the last century, T. rex was pictured as a sluggish, tail-dragging reptile that had to warm up in the sun before it could go anywhere. Then, further research changed that view, replacing it with the active, bird-like animal shown in the movie Jurassic Park. But whether T. rex used warm blood to power that activity remained a question. Now we might have gotten closer to an answer.

A team of researchers led by Randon J. Flores and Robert A. Eagle, geochemists at the University of California, Los Angeles, has measured the T. rex body temperature by analyzing its teeth. This dental thermometer read about 36° Celsius—roughly the body temperature of a modern elephant.

Paleontologists have long argued about dinosaur physiology based on indirect evidence like bone microstructure, growth rates, and where fossils turn up on the map. Some studies suggested many dinosaurs were endotherms, generating their own body heat like birds and mammals. Others argued that each lineage may have had its own thermal strategy.
c8b1edd33ed5a316: Microsoft has a problem not entirely of its own making: The time it takes to bring a system back up to date after a few months of slumber. The company is keen to talk up how efficient it plans to make Windows. Not a day goes by without either a Microsoft representative or a fan insisting that Windows 11 is a lot snappier now than it used to be. (Usually they skirt the unfortunate truth that the Windows of yesteryear generally flies on modern hardware compared with the lumbering of today's software). Microsoft recently claimed that it is working to shrink Windows' footprint to the point where 8 GB would be enough to run things acceptably. We can only hope that one shard of light piercing the gloom of today's memory shortages and rising prices is that developers might prioritize efficient RAM use alongside slinging more ads or adding features few users require. However, this vulture's experience this week indicates that there is another area that needs addressing, and that is the number of updates slung out by vendors, and not just Microsoft. A few days ago, I wrote a story about a new way to skip the Microsoft account requirement during setup for the Home edition of Windows 11. At The Register, we like to test these claims thoroughly, so I fired up an x64 Windows laptop to check them out on real hardware, which is where the problems began. We've written before about the curse of updates, but this machine was running Windows 11 and had been up to date less than a year ago. How long could it take to get to the point where it would boot without Windows Update bleating about missed patches? The answer: about seven hours. Along with the huge array of updates for Windows components and the inevitable insistence that a new version of Microsoft's flagship operating system was needed, there were multiple firmware and driver updates and plenty of restarts. And, of course, there was the progress bar of lies and the percentage counter of deceit. In the decades since Microsoft first inflicted progress bars on Windows users, it has singularly failed to make them accurately reflect the, er, progress. "Yeah, so I'm going to stick at 65 percent for about an hour and then jump to 98 percent in 30 seconds before hanging there for another hour. Lol." That this behavior has endured for decades is beyond disappointing. Redmond is far from the only offender, but Windows' ubiquity makes it one of the most visible. To be clear, this was an ordinary Windows device, running a production version of the operating system. It just hadn't been turned on for a few months. The experience highlights a challenge Microsoft and its vendors must address. It's great that, at long last, people are considering code efficiency rather than simply flinging more hardware at badly written applications to make them run acceptably. But attention must also be paid to the constant flow of updates that seem to stem from an "ah well, we can always fix it in production" attitude that pervades the tech industry. Several years ago, the chief of a DevOps project was baffled when I asked him about testing and validation before release. Surely unit testing was sufficient? And the joy of modern development practices meant that if problems arose, an update could be swiftly rolled out. All of which assumes customers will tolerate continual updates, and a potential hours-long wait if, for some reason, they give it a few months between updates. The tech industry is waking up to the need for efficiencies, or at the very least Microsoft is. It also needs to deal with the scourge of update tsunamis. It's all well and good to brag about making your software run on limited resources until an interminable wait undermines the boast while the various widgets and components of a device insist on spending hours giving themselves a thorough update. d78905474687e96c: From Chin Yee Mun

According to demographic transition theory (DDT), birth rates are expected to decline as a society shifts from an agrarian to an industrial economy, with this change affecting the size and composition of its population.
In an agrarian society, birth rates are high but are also accompanied by high death rates. As a result, population growth was minimal in most societies at the time.
This began to change as societies moved towards industrial economies. Better healthcare meant lower death rates, while birth rates remained more or less unchanged.

However, this trend eventually began to change. Besides better healthcare, industrialisation brought urbanisation, improved education, modern lifestyles and, most importantly, changes in values. Individualism took root as industrialisation empowered such a culture.

As a result, birth rates began to decline. This is particularly visible among Malaysian Chinese. The decline in childbirth among the Chinese in Malaysia, as well as elsewhere, became apparent in the 1980s. The total fertility rate (TFR) among Malaysian Chinese women was 3.3 in 1980. Two decades later, it had fallen to 2.1.

According to the WHO, a TFR of 2.1 is generally considered the replacement level needed for a population to maintain its size over the long term, assuming no migration. If the TFR falls below this level, a population will eventually begin to shrink and age.
Unfortunately, the Chinese community’s TFR has continued to decline. Last year, the TFR among Chinese women was 0.8.

Reports from the statistics department show that the number of Malaysian Chinese has been declining since 2021. Migration is certainly one factor contributing to this decline, but the bigger factor is likely the fall in the Chinese birth rate.
In other words, the Chinese population is now at the “free-fall” stage. In DDT, this refers to a possible fifth stage.

According to the theory, some societies may see birth rates increase after the fourth stage, while others may continue to experience declines. Unfortunately, DDT describes these trends but does not explain why they occur.
Based on my analysis of the Chinese community in Malaysia, as well as Chinese communities across the Sinosphere, I believe I can offer an explanation.
For me, the Chinese have moved into hypermodernity. I took this term from Gilles Lipovetsky, who defined hypermodernity as an era characterised by the following:
Hyper-individualism: An intense focus on personal freedom, self-realisation and immediate gratification.
Hyper-consumerism: Consumption driven not only by status, but also by emotional experiences, health, wellness and constant novelty.
Hyper-technologisation: Technology operating at breakneck speed, redefining time, space and human interaction.

At present, particularly among younger Chinese people, hyper-individualism is increasingly evident. This can be observed in their lifestyles, including the pursuit of immediate gratification and an aversion to responsibilities. They are also driven by hyper-consumerism, sometimes consuming beyond their means.
Technology appears to reinforce these tendencies by connecting people while constantly exposing them to new products and experiences designed to provide gratification.
When such behaviour takes hold, values change.
Chinese values traditionally prioritised family, with starting a family often seen as a natural responsibility.

In a hypermodern world, however, this view is becoming less influential. Family can instead be perceived as a burden or an obstacle to personal gratification and the consumption of goods and experiences that provide satisfaction.

Hence, a subculture of anti-familism appears to be growing among Chinese youth. It may have been started by individuals who view the family as an institution that undermines happiness and life satisfaction.
This can be seen on social media, where various videos encourage singlehood and portray marriage as awful or destructive.
When such messages become widespread, they can validate the idea that it is acceptable to remain single, not start a family and not have children.

Hyper-consumerism may also contribute to the perception that raising children is financially unaffordable. For many Chinese families, raising a child is associated with spending on expensive preschools, private schools and universities.
While wanting to provide the best for one’s children is commendable, these expectations can also become a convenient justification for choosing not to have children.

This problem is now spreading to other communities in Malaysia. The Indian community faces a similar problem, with declining birth rates and a shrinking population. Similar trends are also emerging among Malays and the Bumiputera communities in Sabah and Sarawak.

In my view, measures to address or at least contain this problem must go beyond financial incentives. Many developing countries do not face the same low-birth-rate problem, while the issue is particularly pronounced in upper-middle-income and developed countries.
Hence, the problem is not simply about income. It is about the broader social ecology.

We need to bring hypermodernity under control by addressing hyper-individualism, hyper-consumerism and the influence of technology, particularly social media. At the same time, other measures could help create an environment that is more conducive to starting families and having children.
For example, childcare costs could be reduced by allowing childcare centres to operate in or near workplaces.

Tax and financial incentives could also be introduced as part of a broader effort to improve this social ecology, making it more conducive to forming families and having children rather than relying on them as the primary means of addressing the problem.
Chin Yee Mun is an associate professor and the director of the Tun Tan Cheng Lock Institute of Social Studies at Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman.

31fed871e382cf10: Reactions to former prime minister Najib Razak’s conditional pardon have come in fast and furious, with some singling out Pakatan Harapan and DAP’s Hannah Yeoh for abandoning their stance on graft.

Yeoh, as the federal territories minister, sits on the Federal Territories Pardons Board that met on Friday morning. The Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, who presides over the meeting, granted Najib the conditional pardon, according to the legal affairs division of the Prime Ministers' Department.
But before we, the general public, turn into keyboard warriors waiting to pounce on what we deem to be a gross injustice, there are a few things to bear in mind.

First, Najib did not obtain a full pardon. Umno was pushing for it, but Sultan Ibrahim, in his wisdom, thought otherwise. Najib still has to serve his reduced sentence, at home, once he pays RM50 million up front.
This decision is extremely fair when considering that Najib could have received a full pardon like the one obtained by Anwar Ibrahim in 2018.
Second, the conditional pardon is for the conviction in the SRC International case, not for the 1MDB case. This means Najib isn’t going galavanting any time soon.
Third — and this cannot be emphasised enough -- the power to grant pardons lies with the King and not any sitting government.

Yes, government representatives sit on the pardons board, and that is all we know. We will never know what is discussed, as the minutes of the meeting are classified under the Official Secrets Act. And because we don’t know the discussions that took place, it would be unwise to make assumptions.
It is for this very reason we should not be pointing fingers at the government or Yeoh. The King makes his decision based on the discussions held. End of story.
With these three things out of the way, Najib’s conditional pardon however raises two concerns.
One: does house arrest mean he would be able to receive visitors? Would he have access to social media? Access which would allow him to plan his political comeback?
It doesn't sit right with me if Najib is allowed to receive visitors or access to social media. Irrespective of who you are, the rules and regulations of a house arrest should apply equally.
Two: there will no doubt be politicians who want to resign from government because of Najib’s conditional pardon.
Principled maybe, but not necessarily right. Such a sharp response could be construed as defiance of the King’s will. A move that would undoubtedly whip up a racial and religious rhetoric.
So stay on. And if you need to voice your grievances do so politely. The same goes for those who want to hold demonstrations. Don’ go overboard as it would only sully the royal institution.

Politicians being placed under house arrest isn’t a new phenomenon in the world. Prominent figures in other countries have undergone a similar sentence. Najib only has the “honour” of being the first in Malaysia.
Mind you, he wasn’t pardoned for his crimes, and as a citizen I can live with that.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
eb319f129194071d: A middle-aged Chinese woman from an NGO walked into the newsroom, seeking help.
A journalist of Indian descent was assigned to write the story — that of a young Malay girl who urgently needed medical attention.
This story, recounted by FMT executive chairman Nelson Fernandez at a forum recently, would have just been another account of how Malaysians help each other.
But this was different. People of all races came together to answer a call for help by a Chinese, disseminated by an Indian to help a Malay.
Within hours of FMT publishing the story, up to RM150,000 had been pledged, taking little Diya Amanda on her first step towards a normal childhood.
But for Fernandez, it was just another day at the office.
The Malaysia we keep saying we want is already here.
Nobody ever needed a campaign or matching T-shirts to foster unity. Nobody asked who prayed where or what box they ticked on a form.
This was simply a child who needed help.
And people came forward.

Back in 1982, Paul McCartney and Stevie Wonder sang a lovely song about “Ebony and Ivory” living together in perfect harmony. If black and white piano keys could exist in harmony, surely human beings could figure it out too.
More than forty years later, humanity is still working on it.

We, Malaysians, have spent decades talking about unity. We have slogans, campaigns and speeches about it. We have probably printed enough banners about togetherness to wrap around the country several times over.
Yet one of the best demonstrations of Malaysian unity happened without anybody needing to announce it.
Just like the song, maybe harmony doesn’t require every key to sound the same.
I don’t think Malaysia suffers from an absence of harmony. Perhaps we suffer from not seeing enough of it.
That matters because the stories we repeatedly hear about one another influence the nation we are a part of.
If Malaysians constantly encounter one another through anger, suspicion and confrontation, eventually it becomes easy to believe we are fundamentally divided.
This is why Fernandez’s argument about journalism matters beyond journalism.
He wasn’t suggesting difficult stories shouldn’t be told. Nor should they be.
He was asking for something harder: that conflict does not become the only lens through which Malaysians see one another.
We should be able to disagree fiercely without dehumanising others. We should be able to defend what we believe without humiliating someone who believes differently.
And when we report what divides Malaysia, we should not forget the stories that reveal what still holds us together.
That responsibility isn’t just journalists’ anymore.
Every one of us carries a tiny newsroom in our pockets. We decide what gets shared, forwarded and viral-ed.
Fernandez said something else at the New Muslim Community Conference in Kuala Lumpur, that stayed with me:
“Everyone talks about religion, but no one talks about love, compassion and kindness.”
Love. Compassion. Kindness.
Three words that might seem soft beside politics, race, religion and power.
But as I wrote in my previous article, we have grossly misunderstood softness and strength.
It is easy to be kind to people who agree with us and who are similar and familiar. It takes something stronger to extend that kindness to someone who isn’t.
Perhaps Malaysians do not need to agree on everything and maybe agreement was never the point.
Harmony isn’t everyone singing the same note. That’s unison.
Harmony requires difference.
Ebony and ivory don’t create music because they overcame their differences. Their differences are the point.
Malaysia isn’t so different. A unique colourful country like ours was never going to be one note.
I believe we should stop trying to make everyone sound the same and become better at hearing one another instead.
That’s where harmony begins.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
acee002b425c3e43: As Asean’s health ministers gathered in Kuala Lumpur recently, one wonders if they glanced beyond the conference-room window, searched their conscience, and asked the uncomfortable question: when the next haze emergency threatens millions across the region, what will we actually do — beyond declarations and carefully negotiated language?
Another promise to strengthen cooperation cannot be the answer.

For more than two decades, Asean has monitored hotspots, exchanged information and developed regional plans, yet families still receive essentially the same advice when smoke arrives: remain indoors, reduce outdoor activity and wait.

In Serian, Sarawak, the air pollution index reached 519 on Sept 4, triggering a haze emergency. Although that emergency has since been lifted, it exposed the distance between knowing danger is approaching and protecting people from it.

For parents, including me, this is not an abstract failure of regional cooperation. It is watching children breathe air we know may harm them while having little power to protect them. Satellites can identify fires and monitors can show pollution worsening, but information is inadequate unless it activates a response.
The 17th Asean Health Ministers Meeting provided an opportunity to change at least part of this equation. It was not taken up.

Health ministers were not expected to resolve every political, commercial and environmental cause of transboundary haze before leaving Kuala Lumpur, nor take over the responsibilities of their respective environment, forestry and agriculture ministries.
They could, however, have agreed that the health response to haze will no longer be improvised country by country after populations have already been exposed.

A practical outcome would have been an Asean haze health-protection protocol, agreed in principle at this meeting and developed within a fixed timetable. It could establish what every health system must do when predetermined pollution and population-exposure thresholds are crossed, regardless of where the fire originated or whether arguments over responsibility have been resolved.

Such a protocol should begin with common health triggers. Different air-quality indices, monitoring arrangements and public messages make cross-border conditions difficult to compare. Health ministers should agree on a common method of communicating risk, with aligned protective advice for children, pregnant women, older people, outdoor workers and those living with chronic illness.

Crossing an agreed threshold should automatically activate a defined package of protections. These should include public-health warnings, school and workplace measures, restrictions on strenuous outdoor activity, guidance for employers, extended access to essential respiratory medicines and clean-air spaces in severely affected communities.

Hospitals and clinics should have haze surge plans covering staffing, oxygen, inhalers, masks, filtration and referral capacity before each dry season, rather than trying to assemble them when emergency departments are already under pressure.

Asean must also measure the harm differently. Hotspot counts and daily pollution readings describe the environmental event, but they do not tell us how many people were exposed, for how long or with what consequences. A serious regional health response should report population exposure-days, emergency and outpatient attendances, respiratory exacerbations, medicine demand, school closures, working days lost and the impact on vulnerable communities.

This information should feed into an annual Asean haze health review presented jointly to health and environment ministers. Its purpose must not be to produce another regional publication that is politely noted and then shelved. Countries experiencing repeated or prolonged harmful exposure should publish a time-bound improvement plan covering preparedness, population protection and weaknesses in health-system response, with progress reviewed the following year.

None of this requires health ministers to settle the question of entering another country to fight fires. The Asean haze agreement makes external assistance dependent upon the receiving state’s request and consent. Health ministers can nevertheless pre-authorise cooperation within their sphere: cross-border health alerts, epidemiological data sharing, technical assistance, emergency supplies and mutual support. These arrangements should be settled before the dry season, not while smoke is already spreading.

The Asean Lung Health Progress Framework, which is currently being developed offers a useful starting point. It builds upon the integrated lung-health resolution championed by Malaysia and adopted by the World Health Assembly, which calls for whole-of-government and whole-of-society action involving health, environment, labour, education and finance. The framework can incorporate haze exposure, preparedness and measurable health outcomes without pretending to replace environmental regulation.

Sultan of Perak, Sultan Nazrin Shah, speaking at the opening of the National Cancer Congress Malaysia last weekend, drew attention to the environmental conditions affecting the air children breathe. Asean’s health ministers should heed his warning. The haze cannot remain somebody else’s portfolio until breathing difficulties begin appearing in clinics and hospitals.

Before leaving Kuala Lumpur, Asean’s health ministers should have approved the mandate for a regional haze health-protection protocol, identified the institutions responsible for delivering it, set a deadline before the next dry season and required a public progress report.

Asean has spent more than two decades improving its ability to detect fires and monitor smoke. This meeting should mark the point at which those warnings finally begin to produce consistent protection for the people breathing the air.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect the views of FMT.

4d6f002443b01a18: When it comes to AI models, security functions as an afterthought, as evidenced by increased instances of agents hacking organizations and people, and other security mishaps with agents gone rogue. There's also an opportunity here for companies to offer new solutions. This should not come as a shock to anyone, according to cybersecurity investors and accelerator executives. “On one hand, we shouldn’t be surprised that increasingly capable agents are finding creative and sometimes unexpected ways to accomplish their objectives,” Matt Hartman, chief strategy officer at Merlin Group, told The Register. “On the other, we can’t accept harmful behavior as inevitable or unmanageable.” It’s the same story that plays out with every emerging technology, from laptops to cloud, said Todd Graham, managing partner at Microsoft’s M12 venture fund. “Every time we've built a new piece of infrastructure, we've conveniently forgotten the security,” Graham told The Register. Herein lies the opportunity for early-stage security companies. “If laptops were default secure, we wouldn't have CrowdStrike,” Graham said. “If the cloud was default secure, we wouldn't have Wiz. If identity wasn't default secure, we wouldn't have a bunch of Active Directory add-ons and Okta.” When it comes to AI security, “a lot of ships are going to rise with this tide,” he added. What’s different with AI is the speed at which models are advancing. While companies adopted cloud technologies over a period of years, organizations are moving full speed ahead to incorporate agents and other AI tools into their production environments and allow them to access the most business-critical data and applications. Yet they don’t have a strong handle on how to manage, secure, or even identify the agents that are already roving about their systems. “This is a transition happening month over month, and given the rate of change we’re seeing in the market, I’m in no way or shape surprised that this issue has come to a head in a rather dramatic fashion,” Graham said. “The incidents that have occurred - I’m not going to defend them, but they should be a wake up call. This is a moment in time where we need to insert security, and we're just going to have to insert it faster.” 'Ships are going to rise' with the AI tide Hartman joined Merlin after a lengthy career in federal cybersecurity, including senior roles at the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. In his private-sector role, he helps determine which early- to growth-stage cybersecurity companies the group invests in, and then works with these firms to scale their technology across government, critical infrastructure, and other highly regulated markets. “We’re particularly interested in the security layer that governs agent behavior: identity for non-human actors, clear limits on what they can access and do, and an audit trail for actions taken on an agency’s behalf,” he said. “Agencies aren’t just asking how to adopt agents, they’re asking how to constrain them and prove what one did at 2 AM on a Tuesday.” But while “the opportunity is enormous,” startup founders need to do more than just build an agentic AI security product. “AI has made it faster and cheaper than ever to build a product, so the bar for differentiation keeps rising,” Hartman said. “As the cost of building technology falls, the value shifts toward differentiated capabilities and the ability to take them to market. Founders who can do both have a real opportunity to define this category.” Graham also says that end-users are looking for agentic identity and governance products - “I truly believe someone is going to build the next Okta, just as SaaS generated Okta,” - but adds he sees several founders “thinking way too small.” “I’m seeing a lot of companies that are solving a sliver of the problem,” Graham said. “And the reality is, if I'm a CISO for a Fortune 500 company, no way I'm going to go buy 15 things to do one thing. If you look at the standard identity stack that we’ve had for humans for quite some time, it has governance, you know, access control, authorization, access. For agents, someone's going to have to come to us with a solution that does all of the things.” Agentic identity is the next unicorn When it comes to non-human identities, however, that’s a really big, tough ask. Service accounts remain a prime target for hackers because they typically have high privileges and passwords that never expire. Securing these non-human accounts still plagues security teams - and that’s even before agents entered the mix. Beyond agentic identity, AI endpoint security - think of this as CrowdStrike for AI - is another area ripe for inventive startups, Graham said. He says it’s a challenge he would personally tackle as a founder, but he’s been banned from starting any more companies, so that’s not going to happen. “If you have a breach, and you know you get hauled in front of Congress to explain why you didn't have antivirus turned on [or] EDR, you’re going to add AI endpoint pretty quickly to that list,” Graham said. “It feels like a very hot area that is still early enough, if someone wanted to build a quality solution.” Existing endpoint and antivirus vendors “will absolutely” build products to fill this void, he added. “But it does feel like again a moment in time where disruption is coming for everyone, especially those that have you know pre-existing commitments to go solve.” Graham admits he is “worried” about the recent real-world bad behavior by AI agents. “If left unencumbered, if left to its own devices, I am very concerned about where the endpoint is for this,” he said. Still, he’s “comforted” because he’s seen this scenario play out before, with security scrambling to keep up with infrastructure development. Graham also was "pleasantly surprised” by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s now infamous “We Must Pace the Frontier” essay. “I'm not taking the cynical view that it's some sort of grand conspiracy to get around antitrust,” he told us. “I'm a believer that AI is this awesome tool that is going to fundamentally change a lot of lives for the better. But we’ve got to put in the work now,” Graham said. “We've kicked the security can down the road long enough, and now we need to solve it.” ®
a1cbf7fe06316db9: AI infrastructure could generate enough electronic waste by 2050 to fill a line of shipping containers stretching around Earth six times, according to a report that argues existing estimates drastically understate the problem. Previous estimates have focused chiefly on servers and accelerators such as GPUs, which account for just 13 percent of a datacenter's equipment by weight, the report says. Once power, networking, cooling, and other infrastructure are included, the total could be 40 to 60 times higher than the most widely cited academic projections. The report identifies five equipment categories comprising networking, power distribution, backup power systems, servers plus accelerators, and cooling. Together, these add up to about 7,000 metric tons for a reference 100 MW AI bit barn, much of which will have to be replaced when the facility is upgraded, it argues. The report, How Big Is the AI Waste Wave? [PDF], comes from the Basel Action Network (BAN), a nonprofit organization named after the Basel Convention, which controls international movements of hazardous waste and seeks to prevent its transfer from developed to developing countries. BAN's model starts with what the industry says it intends to build and calculates the potential waste implied by that expansion. It estimates that AI infrastructure will generate between 395 million and 617 million tonnes of e-waste from 2025 to 2050. The report says that would fill between 15 million and 23 million shipping containers. Placing 20 million of them end to end would create a line about 244,000 km long, or roughly six times Earth's circumference. The estimate rests on several assumptions. The model supposes that the copper, steel, cooling and power distribution equipment, networking gear, and computing hardware in the latest AI datacenters will be decommissioned within years rather than decades as the technology becomes obsolete. For example, the report says that when a facility replaces racks drawing between 5 and 15 kW with the 50-140 kW racks required for AI workloads, much of its power infrastructure must be ripped out and replaced. A single 100 MW facility contains about 2,700 tonnes of copper in its cabling and busbars alone. GPUs and other AI accelerators are replaced every two to three years, BAN claims, compared with five to seven years for traditional general-purpose servers. The model assumes that owners replace entire servers when upgrading to the latest generation of Nvidia GPUs, for example. BAN argues this is plausible because the OEMs supplying hyperscalers tend to ship complete, preconfigured systems. Other equipment has different replacement cycles: three to four years for networking infrastructure, eight years for power distribution, and five years for both backup power and cooling systems. The 46-page paper is the first in a series. The second will examine how reuse, refurbishment, and repurposing could reduce the volume of e-waste. The third will consider its potential toxicity, including contamination by perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), while the fourth will examine ways to mitigate the risks. No hyperscaler, government, or international body has published a plan for handling AI-driven e-waste on the scale projected, the report says. It adds that there is insufficient infrastructure to process even current volumes safely. "To date the environmental debate around AI has focused on electricity, carbon and water while largely overlooking what happens to the hardware itself," said BAN founder and chief of strategic direction Jim Puckett. "If companies and governments do not begin planning for this new waste tsunami, today's AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing." ®

2e82d59db2fe2f65: For decades, astronomers thought rings were something only giant planets had. That changed in 2013, when a small, dark body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus passed in front of a star and blinked twice on either side of the main event, revealing two narrow rings around an object barely 250 kilometers across. “It was a surprise,” says Pablo Santos-Sanz, an astronomer at the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Granada, Spain. Ever since, the question has been what such rings are made of and how long they can last.

In a recent study, Santos-Sanz and his colleagues used the James Webb Space Telescope to watch the same body, now known as Chariklo, pass in front of a background star again. They found one of its rings had grown denser and the other had almost vanished. We don’t know exactly why.

The technique behind the observation is simple. “We predict when a Solar System object passes in front of a star,” Santos-Sanz said. The starlight dims for a moment, and the shape of that dip reveals the size, shape, and surroundings of the object that caused it. “This is particularly challenging for minor bodies, and more challenging for distant minor bodies,” he said.
